BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) -- A former Colombian congressman who was held hostage in the jungle for more than eight years has escaped -- with the help of a former captor. Oscar Tulio Lizcano was kidnapped on August 4, 2000 near the Colombian town of Riosucio. Oscar Tulio Lizcano, his hair disheveled, appeared too weak to stand for long when he met the news media Sunday, hours after stumbling onto a military patrol -- and freedom. Lizcano suffered from hunger and disease in captivity and endured isolation in the company of leftist rebels who often would not let him talk, he and Colombian authorities said. "Maybe my incoherence is for a lack of speaking," Lizcano told reporters. "I was unable to talk with the guerillas who guarded me." Lizcano said he had little to read in the jungle except "The Odyssey" by Homer. He suffered from malaria and other illnesses and once ate nothing but hearts of palm for six or seven days, said Juan Manuel Santos, the Colombian defense minister. "This is big news for the whole family," said Lizcano's sister, Amparo Lizcano. "We were waiting for the guerrillas to give our brother back alive before he died." The former congressman fled about three days ago with the assistance of one of his captors, a member of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, a leftist rebel force that has been fighting the government for more than 40 years in a war that also has involved right-wing paramilitaries and drug traffickers.  Watch release of FARC hostage » . President Alvaro Uribe appeared on television Sunday with the ex-FARC rebel -- known by the alias "Isaza" -- and said the man will receive compensation and permission to resettle in France with his family. He said that's in keeping with a Colombian government policy that rewards rebels who desert and help hostages gain their freedom. Police officers and soldiers pinpointed the location of the FARC unit holding Lizcano several months ago, Santos said. They monitored the location for about five months and took steps to seal off possible escape routes, he said, as they planned a rescue operation using information gleaned help from a rebel who deserted October 2. Troops started that rescue operation Saturday -- only to discover that "Isaza" and Lizcano had decided on their own to escape. The two men wandered through the jungle for three days and nights before encountering a Colombian army patrol Sunday, said Santos, the defense minister. Lizcano was kidnapped on August 4, 2000 near the Colombian town of Riosucio. He and his former captor stumbled Sunday onto a patrol near the border of the states of Risaralda and Choco, in central Colombia, authorities said. The FARC holds an estimated 750 hostages in Colombia. Its members have justified hostage taking as a legitimate military tactic. The rebels have been battered this year by government raids that killed several top commanders, the death by apparent heart attack of their founder and a wave of desertions. Government commandoes tricked the FARC in July and freed their most prized hostage, the former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, in an elaborate ruse that also liberated three U.S. defense contractors and 11 other hostages. On Sunday, Lizcano offered words of encouragement to those hundreds who remain trapped in the jungle, captives of the FARC. "Hold on. Hold on," he said. "One day you will enjoy your freedom, too." -- CNN's Karl Penhaul contributed to this report .

BOGOTÁ, Colombia (CNN) — A former Colombian congressman who had been held hostage in the jungle for more than eight years has escaped—with the help of a former captor.

Oscar Tulio Lizcano was kidnapped on August 4, 2000, near the Colombian town of Riosucio. On Sunday, hours after stumbling upon a military patrol—and freedom—Lizcano appeared before the news media with disheveled hair and seemed too weak to stand for long.

Lizcano suffered from hunger and disease during his captivity and endured prolonged isolation in the company of leftist rebels who often would not allow him to speak, he and Colombian authorities said.

“Maybe my incoherence is for a lack of speaking,” Lizcano told reporters. “I was unable to talk with the guerrillas who guarded me.”

Lizcano said he had little to read in the jungle except Homer’s *The Odyssey*. He suffered from malaria and other illnesses and, at one point, ate nothing but hearts of palm for six or seven days, according to Colombian Defense Minister Juan Manuel Santos.

“This is big news for the whole family,” said Lizcano’s sister, Amparo Lizcano. “We were waiting for the guerrillas to give our brother back alive before he died.”

The former congressman fled about three days ago with the assistance of one of his captors, a member of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, a leftist rebel group that has been fighting the government for more than 40 years in a conflict that has also involved right-wing paramilitaries and drug traffickers.

President Álvaro Uribe appeared on television Sunday with the former FARC rebel—known by the alias “Isaza”—and said the man would receive compensation and permission to resettle in France with his family. Uribe said the decision was in keeping with a Colombian government policy that rewards rebels who desert and help hostages gain their freedom.

Police officers and soldiers pinpointed the location of the FARC unit holding Lizcano several months ago, Santos said. They monitored the site for about five months and took steps to seal off possible escape routes as they planned a rescue operation, using information gleaned from a rebel who deserted on October 2.

Troops launched that rescue operation Saturday, only to discover that Isaza and Lizcano had already decided to escape on their own. The two men wandered through the jungle for three days and nights before encountering a Colombian army patrol Sunday, Santos said.

Lizcano and his former captor came upon the patrol near the border of the states of Risaralda and Chocó, in central Colombia, authorities said.

The FARC holds an estimated 750 hostages in Colombia. Its members have justified hostage-taking as a legitimate military tactic. The rebel group has been battered this year by government raids that killed several top commanders, the death of its founder from an apparent heart attack, and a wave of desertions.

In July, government commandos deceived the FARC and freed its most prized hostage, former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, in an elaborate ruse that also liberated three U.S. defense contractors and 11 other hostages.

On Sunday, Lizcano offered words of encouragement to the hundreds who remain trapped in the jungle as captives of the FARC.

“Hold on. Hold on,” he said. “One day you will enjoy your freedom, too.”

CNN’s Karl Penhaul contributed to this report.

BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) — A former Colombian lawmaker, held captive in the jungle for over eight years, has managed to get away — aided by one of the rebels who had been guarding him.

Oscar Tulio Lizcano was seized on August 4, 2000, near the Colombian town of Riosucio. On Sunday, just hours after he and his former captor came across a military patrol and reached safety, Lizcano appeared before reporters looking exhausted, with unkempt hair and seemingly too frail to remain standing for long.

Lizcano and Colombian officials said he had endured hunger, illness and long periods of isolation while being held by leftist guerrillas who frequently did not allow him to speak.

“Maybe my incoherence is for a lack of speaking,” Lizcano told journalists. “I was unable to talk with the guerrillas who guarded me.”

He said that during his years in the jungle he had almost nothing to read apart from Homer’s “The Odyssey.” Colombian Defense Minister Juan Manuel Santos said Lizcano suffered from malaria and other diseases, and at one point survived for six or seven days eating only hearts of palm.

“This is big news for the whole family,” said his sister, Amparo Lizcano. “We were waiting for the guerrillas to give our brother back alive before he died.”

Lizcano escaped roughly three days earlier with help from one of his guards, a member of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, known as FARC. The leftist rebel organization has been at war with Colombia’s government for more than four decades, in a conflict that has also included right-wing paramilitary groups and drug traffickers.

On Sunday, President Alvaro Uribe appeared on television alongside the former FARC fighter, who is known by the alias “Isaza.” Uribe said the man would be given a reward and allowed to move to France with his family. The president said the arrangement followed a Colombian government policy that offers benefits to rebels who abandon the insurgency and assist in freeing hostages.

Santos said police and soldiers had identified the location of the FARC unit holding Lizcano several months earlier. Security forces watched the area for about five months and worked to block possible escape routes while preparing a rescue mission, using information obtained from a rebel who deserted on October 2.

Troops launched that operation on Saturday, but then learned that “Isaza” and Lizcano had already chosen to flee on their own. According to Santos, the two men spent three days and nights moving through the jungle before running into a Colombian army patrol on Sunday.

Authorities said Lizcano and the former rebel encountered the patrol near the border between the states of Risaralda and Choco, in central Colombia.

FARC is believed to be holding about 750 hostages in Colombia. The group has defended kidnapping as a valid military strategy. This year, however, the rebels have suffered serious setbacks, including government attacks that killed several senior commanders, the death of their founder from an apparent heart attack, and a surge in defections.

In July, Colombian commandos deceived FARC in a carefully planned operation that freed the group’s most valuable captive, former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt. The same mission also rescued three U.S. defense contractors and 11 additional hostages.

On Sunday, Lizcano sent a message to the hundreds of people still being held in the jungle by FARC.

“Hold on. Hold on,” he said. “One day you will enjoy your freedom, too.”

CNN’s Karl Penhaul contributed to this report.

**BOGOTÁ, Colombia — Breaking News**

Former Colombian congressman **Oscar Tulio Lizcano** has been freed after more than eight years in captivity at the hands of the **Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC)**, Colombian authorities said Sunday, marking another major blow to the guerrilla group after a series of setbacks this year.

Lizcano, who was kidnapped in 2000, emerged from the jungle in western Colombia after escaping with the help of one of his captors, according to officials. He was reported to be in poor health but alive and receiving medical attention.

President **Álvaro Uribe** welcomed the news, calling Lizcano’s freedom a victory for Colombia’s security forces and for families still waiting for loved ones held by the rebels. Defense Minister **Juan Manuel Santos** said the escape reflected growing pressure on FARC units and deepening demoralization within the insurgency.

Lizcano’s release comes months after the dramatic rescue of **Ingrid Betancourt**, the former presidential candidate who was freed in July along with three U.S. contractors and other hostages in a Colombian military operation that stunned the FARC.

Despite the latest release, officials and relatives’ groups say the rebels continue to hold hostages, including members of the security forces and civilians seized for political leverage or ransom. The government has vowed to maintain military pressure while calling on remaining guerrillas to desert and free captives still in the jungle.
